<reason>Both debaters were polished, disciplined, and well-grounded with no fake precision. A (CON) built a real case — regressive shelf-price premium, safety, targeted alternatives — and had cleaner execution, since B suffered two clipped turns. But B (PRO) won the decisive clashes. B demolished A's prepaid-card answer ("a worse cash with fees attached"), correctly separated network outages from blackouts, answered both pressure questions directly ("we do not size a floor by how often people stand on it"; "Yes, plainly"), and dissolved A's innovation dilemma by showing compliance is not evasion. Most importantly, B exposed a live internal tension A never resolved: four speeches arguing cash is costly, shrinking, and rational for stores to drop, followed by a promise that competition guarantees someone always keeps it. A's "fire codes answered real fires" concession handed B the debate's most damaging flip: a guarantee that arrives after exclusion is a condolence, not a guarantee. A's closing insurance frame was excellent and the regressive-premium point partially survived, but A's holdout-gets-richer claim sat uncomfortably with its own premise that serving cash customers is a net cost. B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Q2 forced A to concede the endpoint (legal tender could buy bread nowhere); A answered "a targeted rule would follow — fire codes answered real fires," and B's closing flipped it: "Fire codes followed real fires because people burned first. A guarantee that arrives after the exclusion is not a guarantee; it is a condolence" — compounded by the charge that A cannot argue retailers rationally abandon cash and simultaneously promise they never will.</best_rebuttal>
